variables.name: read_back
variables.description: Nadia read the back of her half of the map under the lobby lamp.

variables.name: has_chalk
variables.description: Nadia chalked a message on the tour board and kept the chalk.

variables.name: has_token
variables.description: Nadia carries the founder's brass token.

variables.name: has_glasses
variables.description: Nadia kept the founder's reading glasses.

nodes.body: Nadia was the sort of girl who read every label in a museum, and tonight it had cost her. She bent to retie her shoe beside the last case, and when she stood up her class was gone. So was the guard, and so were most of the lights of the old Ellery Museum. She ran to the main doors and pushed, but they were locked for the night, and her phone had no signal behind these thick stone walls. Her mum thought she was sleeping over with her best friend Tess, and Tess thought she had gone home sick. Nobody would miss her before morning. The audio guide still hung around her neck, handset thirteen, the one nobody else had wanted. Behind it in the pouch, where the leaflet should have been, someone had tucked half of an old map of the museum, torn down the middle. One corner carried a small brass mark, a circle crossed by two lines. A pencil had ringed a wing she had never seen on any plan of the museum, and beside the ring it said, in square letters: "The founder's hidden collection, start at the mark."

choices.label: Look for another way out of the lobby.

nodes.body: A switch thunked somewhere in the walls, and at the far end of the lobby a row of lights went dark. Then the next row went, and the next, marching toward her. This was the night setting, and in a minute it would reach the last lamp too, the green one over the visitors' book. Under that lamp she could go over the map properly, front and back, while she could still see it. Across the hall stood the tour board, with TODAY'S TOURS in yellow chalk and a fat stub of chalk on its ledge. The guard had to pass that board on his rounds, sooner or later. Another row of lights died, and the dark took one more step toward her.

choices.label: Spread the map under the lamp.
Chalk a message on the tour board.

nodes.body: Nadia spread the map under the green lamp and turned it over, and the back was not blank. Half a sentence in brown ink ran up to the torn edge: "My east wing is not gone, for it has one door left, and that door opens only" and there the tear cut it off. Below it, someone had printed a warning in square pencil letters: "Rope gallery door shuts itself, so WEDGE IT. I sat in there till the cleaners came." Then the lamp clicked off. She folded the map by feel and followed the last glow of moonlight toward the middle of the museum.

choices.label: Follow the moonlight.

nodes.body: The chalk squeaked as Nadia wrote under TODAY'S TOURS, as big as the board allowed: "LOCKED IN, NOT A BURGLAR, NADIA FROM CLASS 6B." She looked at it for a moment and then added, a little smaller, "BACK SOON." The guard would have to laugh at that, or at least not call the police. The last lamp clicked off behind her. She dropped the chalk into her coat pocket, wiped her yellow fingers on her jeans, and followed the last glow of moonlight toward the middle of the museum.

choices.label: Follow the moonlight.

nodes.body: The rotunda was round and tall and full of moonlight. In the middle stood a huge brass globe on a stone pedestal, rings inside rings, as still as it had been all day. A plaque at its foot said 1. Nadia keyed the number into her handset, mostly for the company. "Stop one," chirped a bright voice. Then came the founder himself, old Ambrose Ellery, who had recorded his own tour almost a hundred years ago. "A museum ought to have a heart," said old Ellery, crackling like a fire, "and mine is brass, and you are looking at it. Most people look for four seconds, so do better." Three archways led off under three brass signs: the Gallery of Gems, the Egyptian Wing, and the stairs down to the Archive.

choices.label: Slip into the Gallery of Gems.
Head for the Egyptian Wing.
Try the old Archive downstairs.

nodes.body: The Gallery of Gems glittered under its low night lights. Every ring and stone threw off a tiny spark of color. A plaque by the door said 12, so Nadia keyed it in. "Stop twelve," said the handset, and then Ellery came on, as dry as old paper. "I never cared for diamonds, which are too pleased with themselves," he said, "but people will walk a mile to look at one, and I needed people." In the middle of the room a big glass case of gems sat crooked on its stand, as if someone had bumped it and not looked back. From somewhere past it came a soft beeping, faint and steady, like a clock that had learned one word.

choices.label: Study the big crooked case.
Follow the faint beeping.

nodes.body: Up close, the big crooked case told on somebody. A hand had opened it in a hurry and shut it just as fast, leaving a smear across the dusty glass and the little door unlatched. Inside, among the gems, one small glass vitrine sat tilted on its stand, as if something was wedged beneath it. Behind it a little card had fallen face down on the shelf. Both had been moved, and not long ago, because dust takes years and a smear takes a second. "Somebody else has been looking," Nadia told the handset, which had nothing to say about that.

choices.label: Look under the tilted vitrine.
Read the little card that fell behind.

nodes.body: Nadia reached in and tipped the tilted vitrine back on its stand. Under it lay the thing that had made it lean: a brass token the size of a coin, stamped with the mark from her map, a circle crossed by two lines. Four words ran around its other side: "LEAVE ME WHERE YOU TAKE." Nadia frowned at it and said, "Take what?" The token did not say, so she put it in her pocket anyway. Where it had lain, an arrow was scratched into the wood, and it pointed at the back wall, where a narrow door stood half hidden behind a folded screen.

choices.label: Follow the arrow to the narrow door.

nodes.body: Nadia turned the little card over and read it. It was an old exhibit label, its ink gone brown, written in a thin hand that she guessed was the founder's own. "This ring is glass, and the real one went somewhere safer," it said, "and so did a good deal else, so if you are the curious sort, try the corridor." The last word was underlined twice. She checked her half of the map and found a narrow corridor running behind the gallery, with its door in the back wall, half hidden by a folded screen. "The curious sort," Nadia said to the card, "would be me."

choices.label: Head for the corridor door.

nodes.body: The narrow corridor smelled of dust and old floor polish, and her footsteps came back to her a beat late. Empty shelves lined both walls. There was no plaque here, and the handset had nothing to say about the place, which felt like a clue all by itself. The corridor ended in a blank wall, and she almost turned around before she saw it. Low down, where the wall met the floor, the mark from her map was scratched into the skirting board. The board sat loose, with its edge lifted just enough to slide a finger under.

choices.label: Pry up the loose skirting board.

nodes.body: Nadia followed the beeping past three cases of rings and one of rough, uncut stones. It came from a small panel on the wall, blinking amber beside a wide stone plinth, and it was only a sensor with a tired battery. She was still looking at it when a torch beam swung into the far end of the gallery. It was the night guard, checking case after case, slow and steady, and humming to himself. If he found her, the night was over, because he would walk her to the lobby and the map would go in a drawer. The beam slid closer. On her other side stood a row of white marble busts, each one wearing a necklace.

choices.label: Duck behind the stone plinth.
Stand among the marble busts, still as a statue.

nodes.body: Nadia ducked behind the plinth and folded up small, with her knees against her chest. The torch beam swept the spot where she had been standing and moved on, and the guard's shoes squeaked past. He stopped at the big crooked case. "Evening, you old show-off," he said to the largest diamond, "and I suppose you still have nothing to tell me, after thirty-one years of asking." He sighed, and his steps faded toward the far doors. Thirty-one years of asking for what? When Nadia looked up, a narrow door in the back wall stood open a crack, as if he had just looked in there on his rounds.

choices.label: Slip through the narrow door.

nodes.body: The Egyptian Wing was full of long shadows and painted eyes. Carved faces watched from every wall, and a plaque by the door said 19. Nadia keyed it in. "Stop nineteen," said the handset, and Ellery crackled awake. "The lady in the painted box has been dead three thousand years," he said, "and she is still the best listener in the building, so tell her nothing you want kept." The painted sarcophagus stood in the middle of the room. Its lid sat a little crooked, wrong for something meant to stay shut. On the wall beyond hung a faded map of the museum as it was a hundred years ago, with halls on it that Nadia had never walked.

choices.label: Examine the painted sarcophagus.
Trace the wall map of the old museum.

nodes.body: The sarcophagus lid was heavier than it looked. It sat off its base by a thumb's width, as though someone had lifted it and not set it back straight. Nadia put both hands on the cool painted wood and felt it shift. "Sorry," she whispered to the lady inside, "but I think somebody got here before me." A few steps away stood the amulet case, where small charms rested each in its own dent of dark velvet. One dent sat empty, round and no bigger than a coin, and the velvet still held the shape of whatever had gone.

choices.label: Peek under the loose lid.
Check the amulet case.

nodes.body: Nadia eased the loose lid up another inch and slid her hand under it. The inner case was shut tight, but on top of it sat a nest of yellowed cotton, and in the cotton lay something small and hard. It was a brass token the size of a coin, stamped with the mark from her map, a circle crossed by two lines. Four words ran around its other side: "LEAVE ME WHERE YOU TAKE." Nadia looked at it and said, "I just did the opposite," and put it in her pocket. She let the lid settle. A thin draught touched her cheek, cool and steady, from a gap in the wall behind the sarcophagus.

choices.label: Follow the draught to the hall.

nodes.body: The amulet case had a card for every charm, and a card for the empty dent too. It was written in a thin, old-fashioned hand: "Token of the house, removed by the founder, who is allowed to steal from himself, and it is not far away." Nadia looked back at the sarcophagus, then down at the glass. A thin arrow was scratched right into it, so faint that she saw it only when the light caught the edge. It pointed past the sarcophagus to a gap in the wall, where a hall opened into the dark. "Not far away," she said, "and that is all you are going to tell me, isn't it?"

choices.label: Follow the scratched arrow to the hall.

nodes.body: The hall behind the wing was bare. It had gray walls, a bucket of sand, and half a dozen rusted tools leaning in a corner like men waiting for a bus. There was no plaque here. The handset had nothing to say about the place, and that felt like a clue all by itself. At the far end, one floor tile carried the mark from her map, a circle crossed by two lines, cut into the stone. Nadia stepped on it, and the tile rocked under her shoe, looser than the tiles around it.

choices.label: Lift the rocking floor tile.

nodes.body: Nadia traced a finger across the old wall map. One wing on it matched no floor plan she had ever seen. It was the wing ringed in pencil on her own half of the map, and it began right behind this room. A torch hung on a bracket nearby, the kind kept for power cuts. To her left a red rope barred the door of a dark gallery, and a card on the rope said CLOSED FOR REPAIR, in letters so faded that the repair must have been planned for her grandmother. Cold air came from under that door, and it smelled of plaster dust.

choices.label: Take the torch and follow the wall map.
Duck under the rope into the dark gallery.
Wedge the gallery door open, then duck under the rope.

nodes.body: Nadia lifted the torch from its bracket and clicked it on, and a thin beam cut the dark. She followed the lost wing just as the wall map drew it, out past the sarcophagus, round a turn she had never noticed, and into a hall she had surely never walked in daylight. The roped gallery fell behind her, and whatever was in there could keep its repairs. The beam ran ahead over bare gray walls and caught a glint in the floor at the far end. Then it turned orange, then brown, and died, because a power-cut torch has a power-cut battery. She set it down and walked on.

choices.label: Walk toward the glint.

nodes.body: Nadia dragged a brass rope post into the gallery doorway and wedged it flat across the sill. Whoever wrote that warning had sat in here till the cleaners came, and she did not plan to. She ducked under the rope, and behind her the door swung, hit the post, and stayed open, grumbling. The gallery held dust sheets, a ladder, and one huge arch, bricked up, with a number painted on the bricks. It was 29, so she keyed it in. "Stop twenty-nine," said the handset, and Ellery said, "Through this arch lies my east wing, the best rooms in the house." Cold air leaked between the bricks, so the wing was still back there. A side door let her out of the gallery by the back way.

choices.label: Step out into the hall.

nodes.body: The Archive smelled of old paper and older dust. Nobody had opened a window down here in years. Nadia keyed in the number painted by the door. "Stop thirty-one," said the handset, and Ellery cleared his throat. "Every museum has a memory," he said, "and ours is this archive, down where it is cool, which forgets nothing except where it put things." Two reading lamps made a small pool of light. In it, a visitor ledger lay open on a wooden stand, its pages soft and curling. Beyond the lamps the back stacks ran off into the dark, shelf after shelf, so deep that Nadia could not see where they stopped.

choices.label: Open the dusty visitor ledger.
Push into the unlit back stacks.

nodes.body: Nadia turned the pages of the dusty ledger backward, through a hundred years of visitors. There were school trips and scholars, and a man who had signed himself only as "tired". On the very first page one name stood alone, the founder's own, and beside it, in the column that asked why he had come, he had written: "To hide something." She grinned. Next to the stand stood a card index, its small drawers labeled in fading ink. Under it sat a low cabinet with one deep bottom drawer, and when she tugged the handle it stuck fast, and something inside it rolled and clinked.

choices.label: Check the card index.
Try the sticking bottom drawer.

nodes.body: Nadia walked her fingers through the card index until one card stopped her. It was filed out of order, and stamped in the corner with the mark from her map, a circle crossed by two lines. A thin hand ran across it: "I have filed this under Q, where nobody looks, so go to Row Q, at the far end of the back stacks, behind the dictionaries." She slid the card back and turned to the dark shelves of the archive. White letters were painted on the shelf ends, just bright enough to read by the last spill of lamplight.

choices.label: Follow the letters to Row Q.

nodes.body: Nadia braced her feet and pulled, and the bottom drawer gave with a groan. Something rolled to the front and spun to a stop. It was a brass token the size of a coin, stamped with the mark from her map, a circle crossed by two lines. Four words ran around its other side: "LEAVE ME WHERE YOU TAKE." Nadia picked it up, told it, "A bit late for that," and put it in her pocket. Under it lay a folded plan of the stacks, soft with age, with one shelf ringed in heavy pencil, in Row Q. White letters marked the shelf ends out in the dark, just bright enough to follow.

choices.label: Head for the ringed shelf.

nodes.body: Row Q was the last row, and the dustiest. Halfway along it, at knee height, her fingers found a mark cut into the edge of a shelf: a circle crossed by two lines. A row of fat old dictionaries stood on that shelf, shoulder to shoulder, and nobody had opened one in years. Nadia ran her hand along their tops. Behind them she felt a gap, just wide enough for her fingers if she pushed her arm in sideways and did not think too hard about spiders.

choices.label: Reach into the gap behind the books.

nodes.body: The back stacks swallowed the lamplight in three steps. Nadia stood at the edge of true dark, with shelves running away on both sides. Something round and heavy hung from a hook to her left, about the size of an old battery lantern. But a grating overhead opened on the lobby floor, and a light down here would shine up through it like a flag for the guard to see. The shelves were straight, at least. A person might keep one hand on them and count.

choices.label: Take down the lantern and switch it on.
Go on in the dark, counting shelves by hand.
Chalk an arrow on every shelf end and go on in the dark.

nodes.body: Nadia took the lantern down off its hook and thumbed the switch. Warm light spread across the nearest shelves, and she stood very still and looked up at the grating. There was no shout from above, and no sound of running feet. White letters showed on the shelf ends now, marching off into the dark, and she followed them all the way to the last one. She hung the lantern on the end of the row, where it lit the whole length of the shelves, and went in.

choices.label: Search the last row.

nodes.body: Nadia took the chalk from her pocket and drew a fat arrow on the first shelf end, pointing back at the lamps. Then she walked into the dark and did it again at every corner, ten arrows, then eleven. At the twelfth her hand met a shelf of flat boxes, and she spent one second of phone light on them. They were gramophone records, labeled in a thin hand: "The Founder's Tour, 1 to 36." Four more boxes sat apart, marked 37 to 40, and their label said: "For the finder." Nadia stared at them. "There are only thirty-six stops," she said, and nobody argued. In the same second of light she read the white letter on the next shelf end. It was Q.

choices.label: Turn into Row Q.

nodes.body: Her fingers closed on something wrapped in cloth. Nadia drew it out and unrolled a scrap of oilcloth, stiff with age, and inside lay a small brass key with the mark from her map stamped on its head. A note was tied to it with string, covered in neat rows of letters that spelled nothing at all, which had to be a code. There was a brass tag as well, stamped 37, although the museum's stops ended at 36. She keyed it in anyway. "Stop thirty-seven," said the handset, as if that were nothing, and then Ellery said, "So you found my key. It fits three locks, and all of them lead to my rooms at the top of the house: my study, my glass cabinet, and my back stair. Behind each one I left a way to read that note, so choose as you please, for I was never a man for one door."

choices.label: Try the key on the founder's study door.
Try the key on the glass cabinet.
Try the key on the back stair door.

nodes.body: The key turned in the study door with a stiff click. Nadia pushed, and the door opened on a room that smelled of sealed time, with dust lying thick on everything. A roll-top desk stood against one wall, its curved cover half raised like a sleepy eye. Above it hung a painted portrait of the founder, with a white beard, a sharp nose, and dark eyes that seemed to follow her. So that was the face that went with the voice. "You look crosser than you sound," she told it. The portrait hung a little away from the wall on one side, as if it had been opened like a door.

choices.label: Search the roll-top desk.
Look behind the founder's portrait.

nodes.body: Nadia searched the roll-top desk, row after row of small pigeonholes, past old letters and dried-out pens. At the back she found a slim leather notebook with a pair of round glasses folded on top. The notebook's writing was the size of ants. She put the glasses on, and the ants stood up and became words. The first page held a line of the same code as her note, with its plain meaning penciled underneath. He had shown his working, once, and left the rest to her. She pushed the glasses up into her hair and carried the notebook out to the landing, where a small reading table stood by the window.

choices.label: Carry the notebook to the reading table.

nodes.body: Nadia eased the heavy portrait away from the wall, and it swung on a hinge like a door. Behind the founder's face sat a shallow safe, already open, with one thing on its shelf. It was a small brass wheel with two rings of letters, one inside the other, and the inner ring still turned smoothly under her thumb. It was a wheel for turning one alphabet into another. "Thank you," she told the portrait, which looked as cross as ever. She carried the cipher wheel out to the landing, where a small reading table stood by the window.

choices.label: Take the cipher wheel to the table.

nodes.body: The glass cabinet stood on the landing outside the study, against the far wall. Under its lid lay a stack of the founder's travel journals, their leather covers cracked and soft. Nadia fitted the brass key to the latch, and it turned with a neat click, but the lid was another matter. A hundred years of dust and dried varnish had glued the hinge almost solid, and when she pushed, it barely moved. Somewhere below her, keys jingled. The guard was on the main stairs, humming, and getting louder.

choices.label: Ease the lid open, a little at a time.
Shove the lid up before he gets here.

nodes.body: Nadia eased the lid from side to side instead of pushing it straight up, working the old hinge loose a little at a time. The humming climbed the stairs, and she kept rocking. Then the humming reached the top step, paused, and turned away down the long gallery, and the keys faded with it. The lid came free without a sound. Tucked among the travel journals lay a slim ledger with a faded ribbon marking one page, and it looked like a thing left for somebody patient.

choices.label: Lift out the bookmarked ledger.

nodes.body: The ribbon marked a page ruled in two columns. Down one side ran the alphabet. Down the other ran the alphabet again, in the same neat hand as the note on her key, but it started at D. Every letter sat three places on from its partner. It was a table for swapping one letter for another, and it was exactly what the note needed. Nadia shut the ledger on her finger to keep the place. By the landing window stood a small reading table with a green-shaded lamp, as if the spot had been laid out for this.

choices.label: Spread the ledger on the reading table.

nodes.body: Nadia put her shoulder under the lid and shoved, and it rose a hand's width and stuck there, and the old glass let out a long, low creak, the sound glass makes while it decides whether to bend or break. On the stairs the humming stopped. "Is somebody up there?" called the guard, and his keys began to jingle faster. Through the gap under the lid she could see a slim ledger with a ribbon in it, almost close enough to touch.

choices.label: Let the lid down and start again, gently.
Give the lid one hard pull and grab the ledger.

nodes.body: Nadia let the lid down, as slow as breathing, and the creak faded. Then she crouched behind the cabinet and waited while a torch beam crossed the ceiling. "Old house," the guard told himself at last, "always talking in its sleep," and his keys went away down the stairs. This time she rocked the lid gently from side to side until the hinge gave with a sigh, and a ribboned ledger slid into her hands. Its marked page held two columns, the alphabet and the alphabet again, starting three letters on. It was a table for swapping letters. She carried it to a small reading table by the landing window and pulled the chain of its green-shaded lamp. Green light fell across the table, so someone had been changing the bulb. She untied the note from her key.

choices.label: Start on the code.

nodes.body: The back stair door hid behind the cloakroom, painted the same gray as the wall. The key slid into its lock and turned with a heavy clunk. The door swung in on a narrow stairwell that rose to a landing lost in shadow, and cool air came down to meet her. At the foot of the stairs, tucked beside the bottom step, stood a small cupboard with its door hanging open a crack. Something pale showed in the gap.

choices.label: Climb toward the landing.
Check the cupboard by the bottom step.

nodes.body: Nadia climbed toward the landing one careful step at a time, with a hand on each wall. At the top she found a window, a small reading table, and a door marked STUDY, so this was the back way into the founder's rooms. Set into the wall at the head of the stairs was a brass dial as big as a saucer, with two rings of letters, one inside the other. The inner ring turned under her hand until A met D and B met E. It was a simple trick once she saw it. Every letter had stepped three places on. She did not need to carry the dial, only to remember it.

choices.label: Sit at the reading table.

nodes.body: Nadia crouched and opened the cupboard the rest of the way. Inside lay a rolled chart, brittle at the edges, and a pair of round glasses with thick lenses. She unrolled the chart a little and found two rings of letters drawn on it, one inside the other, like a clock with an alphabet for hours. Beneath them ran a line of writing too small to read. She tried the glasses on, and the tiny line jumped up clear: "Turn the inner ring three places, and good luck to you." She pushed the glasses up into her hair, tucked the chart under her arm, and climbed to the landing at the top.

choices.label: Carry the chart to the reading table.

nodes.body: The lamp on the reading table had a brass chain. Nadia pulled it, not hoping for much, and green light fell across the little table, so someone had been changing the bulb. She sat down, untied the note from the key, and pressed it flat under the lamp. It held rows of letters, as neat as a times table, and not a word among them. "All right," she said to the founder, wherever he was, "show me."

choices.label: Start on the first line.

nodes.body: Letter by letter, Nadia worked the code loose. Each letter stepped three places back, so every D became an A. She crossed out two false starts and tried again, and then the first line fell open all at once: "Follow the stars to the heart of my house." The heart had to be the brass globe in the rotunda, the one she had looked at for four seconds. The rest came faster: "It sleeps until one of my three roads wakes it, so come by the Astronomy Hall, the Map Room, or the Clock Corridor, and then set its rings to four, nine, and two." Nadia read it over until the numbers stuck. Then she folded the note into her pocket and switched off the lamp.

choices.label: Take the road through the Astronomy Hall.
Take the road through the Map Room.
Take the road down the Clock Corridor.

nodes.body: The Astronomy Hall glimmered under a vast painted dome, with gold stars flaking off deep blue plaster. A plaque said 22, and Nadia keyed it in. "Stop twenty-two," said the handset. "I had the sky painted as it stood on the night we opened," said Ellery, "and one of those stars is a liar, though I shall not say which." A spiral stair wound up the curved wall toward the painted stars, slow and grand. Off to one side, half hidden behind a curtain, a plain metal ladder ran straight up into the dark, with a sign on a chain that said STAFF ONLY.

choices.label: Climb the spiral stair to the painted stars.
Take the staff ladder behind the curtain.

nodes.body: Nadia climbed the spiral stair until she stood just under the painted sky, close enough to see the brush strokes in the gold. One of those stars was a liar. She walked along the top step with a hand on the rail, looking at each star in turn, and found it at last. One star was not paint at all, but a brass stud the size of a thumbnail. A thin painted line ran from it down the wall to a small door she would never have noticed. She pressed the star, and the door clicked open on a passage that sloped down toward the middle of the museum.

choices.label: Take the passage behind the star.

nodes.body: Nadia took the staff ladder, which was cold and a little rusty and went up farther than it looked. It ended at a caged walkway bolted across the hall, right under the dome, with rails on both sides. From up here the gold stars were as big as dinner plates. At the far end of the walkway a small door waited in the wall. But a second ladder went on from the cage, bare rungs climbing into the dark top of the dome, where no stars were painted at all. A sign hung on it, too rusted to read.

choices.label: Cross the caged walkway to the door.
Climb higher into the dark dome.

nodes.body: Nadia crossed the caged walkway one step at a time, with both hands on the rails and her eyes on the door. Halfway over, one gold star on the dome beside her caught the light in a way the others did not. It was not paint. It was a brass stud, and a thin line ran from it along the wall to the very door she was walking toward. So that was the liar. She pressed it as she passed, and ahead of her the door clicked open on a narrow stair that led down, with cool air rising to meet her.

choices.label: Go down the narrow stair.

nodes.body: The Map Room was papered from floor to ceiling with old charts, faded to soft browns and blues. A plaque by the door said 25, and Nadia keyed it in. "Stop twenty-five," said the handset. "A map is a promise," said Ellery, "and most of them are broken, but mine are not." In the middle of the room stood a great floor globe, taller than Nadia, set on brass rails so that it turned at a touch. It was not a globe of the world. It was a globe of the night sky, black, and pricked all over with silver stars. Nearby a giant atlas lay open on a slanted stand, with pages nearly as wide as she was tall.

choices.label: Spin the great floor globe.
Turn the pages of the giant atlas.

nodes.body: Nadia set both palms on the great globe and spun it slowly. Silver stars slid past under her hands, hundreds of them, each no bigger than a pinhead, and one of them was gold. She turned the globe until the gold star sat under the brass pointer at the top, and then she let go. Something clicked deep inside, small and exact, like a key turning in a clock. Along the foot of the nearest wall a low panel swung aside on a hinge. Behind it a narrow passage ran off toward the middle of the museum, breathing cool air.

choices.label: Duck through the low panel.

nodes.body: Nadia turned the giant atlas's pages, coast after coast, until the countries ran out and the last pages became star charts. One chart was not printed. It was drawn by hand in thin brown ink, and it was not the sky at all. It was this museum, with every room a little star, all joined up like a constellation. A route ran through it in faded red, past rooms she knew and rooms she did not, to one large star in the middle. Under that star the founder had written: "You are nearly there, so mind the crates."

choices.label: Follow the inked red route.

nodes.body: Nadia followed the red route just as it was drawn. It took her down a back stair she would never have found alone and into a store room stacked to the ceiling with crates. She minded the crates. The path bent twice, as the chart had promised, and ended at a plain door with a tiny gold star painted over the handle. She put her palm flat on the wood for a moment. Part of her still expected a broom cupboard on the other side.

choices.label: Open the door with the gold star.

nodes.body: The Clock Corridor ticked with a hundred old clocks, each a little out of step with the rest, so that the air itself seemed to hum. Nadia keyed in the number on the wall. "Stop twenty-seven," said the handset. "I built most of these," said Ellery, "and they disagree about the time, as did everyone I ever met." At one end of the corridor a small door stood open on a gear room, where the real machinery lived. At the other end a tall clock stood over a second doorway, and its great brass pendulum swung slow and heavy right across the gap.

choices.label: Follow the ticking to the gear room.
Cross under the great pendulum.

nodes.body: Nadia followed the ticking into the gear room, which smelled of oil and warm metal. Wheels turned quietly behind glass, and in the middle stood the master clock that drove them all. Its face had no numbers. Twelve small stars were painted round it instead, eleven of them silver and one gold, and the hands sat a little way short of the gold one. The note had said to follow the stars. She opened the glass and walked the minute hand forward with one fingertip, and then the hour hand, until both pointed at the gold star. Under her feet something clicked and let go, and a narrow door swung open in the far wall.

choices.label: Go through the narrow door.

nodes.body: The pendulum was a brass disc as wide as a dustbin lid, and it swung right across the doorway at that end of the corridor. Each pass pushed a soft wall of air against Nadia's face. There was no way round it. On its far swing the pendulum hung for a long moment, well clear of the door, as if it were holding its breath, and then it came back with a tick. A gold star was painted on the floor just past the doorway. She counted the beat under her breath, one, two, three, and her legs wanted to go on every one.

choices.label: Learn the pendulum's beat, then walk through.
Dash through while the pendulum hangs clear.

nodes.body: Nadia counted the pendulum's beat once more, to be sure she had learned it. On three the disc swung away, and she walked through, steady and not running, right on the rhythm. It came back behind her with a soft whoosh and missed her by a comfortable arm's length. She stepped over the gold star on the floor. Beyond it a plain passage sloped gently down, and the ticking faded behind her with every step.

choices.label: Follow the sloping passage.

nodes.body: The last door opened on moonlight and marble, and Nadia stepped out into the rotunda. As the door swung wide, a wire somewhere under the floor pulled tight. Out in the middle of the room a brass pin slid from the great globe and rang on the stone like a dropped coin, and the rings shivered, free. The heart of the house was awake. Nadia walked all the way round it, slowly this time, and counted three rings, each numbered like a clock, above a stone pedestal carved all over with small square tiles. Across the hall, a door she had not noticed by day stood ajar, with NIGHT GUARD painted on it and a gray light flickering inside. The room seemed empty.

choices.label: Set the rings of the globe to four, nine, and two.
Search the carved pedestal.
Slip into the night guard's room.

nodes.body: Nadia put her hands on the outer ring of the globe. It turned with barely a whisper, smoother than anything that old had a right to be. The numbers on the rings were worn almost flat, and by the glow of her phone a four looked a good deal like a nine. The rings were eager, too, so that a touch too much sent them sliding right past the mark. Deep inside the globe something ticked each time a number went by, as soft as a safe in a film.

choices.label: Check each worn number twice, then set the rings.
Turn each ring by ear, listening for the tick.

nodes.body: One ring at a time, Nadia set the worn numbers against the pointer. She checked each one twice by the light of her phone, and once more with a fingertip, before she let go. When the last ring clicked home on the two, the whole globe seemed to sigh, and gears meshed somewhere deep inside it. A slab of marble beside the pedestal shuddered and slid back. Under it a narrow stair wound down into the dark, and cool air came up to meet her, smelling of stone and old paper.

choices.label: Descend the hidden stair.

nodes.body: Nadia shut her eyes and turned each ring by ear, listening for the tick. One tick always sounded deeper than the rest, and she stopped on it three times, feeling clever. It was wrong. The rings clunked together with a sound like a complaint, and the globe let out a low groan, and nothing opened. Worse, the third ring had caught on something inside. It sat a finger's width short of the two, close enough to see, and it refused to turn back, although one good shove ought to carry it over.

choices.label: Work the third ring loose and start again.
Shove the third ring over the last finger's width.

nodes.body: Nadia worked the third ring loose a hair at a time, until it came free with a click. Then she wound all three rings back to twelve and made herself slow down. She read the numbers off the note out loud, like a shopping list: "Four, nine, two." This time she used her eyes instead of her ears. When the last ring clicked home, the gears meshed clean, and a slab of marble beside the pedestal slid back. A narrow stair wound down into the dark, just where the heart of the house had been hiding it.

choices.label: Take the stair down.

nodes.body: The pedestal under the globe was carved all over with small square tiles, and when Nadia pushed one, it slid. Each tile carried a scrap of line or curve, worn smooth by years of fingers, or by one very patient founder. She ran her hand on round the base and stopped. One seam breathed against her palm, a thin cold draught that had no business in solid stone. It came from the wall side, where a low door hid in the curve of the rotunda, painted the same white as the wall.

choices.label: Slide the tiles into a picture.
Follow the draught to the low door.

nodes.body: Nadia slid the tiles one at a time, matching curve to curve and line to line. She had seen this picture all night. When the last tile clicked home, the pedestal showed the mark from her map, a circle crossed by two lines, as wide as her hand. A catch let go inside the stone with a soft snap. Beside the pedestal a slab of marble drew back, and a narrow stair wound down into the dark.

choices.label: Go down the hidden stair.

nodes.body: Nadia followed the draught across the floor to the low door in the curve of the wall. No floor plan had ever shown it, and its hinges were stiff but willing. Beyond it lay a small, dusty room crowded with workbenches and glass domes, and under every dome stood something half built from brass. A number was chalked on the door frame in a thin hand, and it was 39.

choices.label: Step into the hidden room.

nodes.body: She stepped into the hidden room and keyed the number in. "Stop thirty-nine," said the handset. "So you have found where I hid from my own museum," said Ellery, and for once he sounded pleased. "Touch what you like, for they are only half finished, and so was I." Benches ran along every wall, crowded with brass birds and clockwork beasts frozen in the middle of a gesture, each one labeled in his thin hand. There was no gold in here, and there were no jewels. On the nearest bench sat a brass wren no bigger than her thumb, with a key in its back.

choices.label: Wind the brass wren.

nodes.body: The night guard's room hummed with a bank of old screens, each showing an empty hall in flickering gray. His chair was still warm. On the desk a thick rounds book lay open, its pages filled with tidy times and the same two initials, over and over, going back years. Beside it sat a mug of cold tea, a folded crossword, and a heavy black phone with a coiled cord. None of the screens showed where he had gone.

choices.label: Turn the rounds book back to its first page.
Pick up the black phone.
Unfold the crossword with NADIA printed on it.

nodes.body: Nadia turned the rounds book back to its very first page, which was not in a guard's hand at all. "Rule for the night watch," the founder had written. "At a quarter to four each morning, stand clear of the globe, because if the heart is awake, my clockwork brings the rings home by itself and opens the floor. Tell no one." Under it, a long line of guards had signed, and the last of them had added in square pencil letters, "Never seen it." Nadia looked at the clock over the door, which said sixteen minutes to four, and she ran. The marble was already sliding back when she reached the globe.

choices.label: Descend the opened stair.

nodes.body: Nadia unfolded the crossword, which he had left on top of the rounds book. Across its white edge he had printed in square pencil letters: "NADIA (NOT A BURGLAR), I saw your board and have looked in every room twice. I cannot find you, so you must be somewhere I have never been, and good for you. The front doors are unlocked, and I am at the front desk with the kettle on, so come and ring your mother." It was signed "Pym, the night guard," and under that he had added, "If you have my map, I should like to know how far you got." Nadia pulled out the map, and the square pencil letters on it were the same.

choices.label: Walk out to the front desk.
Stay hidden and read the rounds book.

nodes.body: The night guard sat at the front desk with a flask, two mugs, and another crossword, and he was older than Nadia had pictured, with a white moustache and a cardigan under his uniform jacket. "Not a burglar, seven letters, begins with V," he said, without looking up. Nadia thought about it. "Visitor," she said, and he wrote it in. Then he looked at her, and at the brass key in her hand, and he put his pencil down very slowly. "Thirty-one years I have hunted for that," said Mr. Pym, "so where was it?" She told him all of it, from the shoelace onward. "Your mother first," he said, pushing the desk phone across to her, "and then you can show an old man a thing or two."

choices.label: Ring home, then lead the way.

nodes.body: Nadia picked up the black phone, and to her surprise a dial tone hummed in her ear. It was the first ordinary sound she had heard all night. At the far end of that hum were her own kitchen, a warm car, and her bed. Behind her, through the open door, the brass globe stood waiting with its pin on the floor, and she knew the three numbers that would open it. Her thumb found the first button of her home number and rested there.

choices.label: Dial the rest of the number.

nodes.body: The stair let Nadia out into a low stone room, lit only by the glow of her phone. Shelves lined every wall, crowded with paintings and carvings and small glinting things, all of it under a hundred years of dust. Over the door someone had carved the number 38, and she keyed it in with a thumb that would not hold still. "Stop thirty-eight," said the handset. "Welcome, finder," said Ellery. "Every piece in this room belongs to the town, and I only hid it from men who meant to sell it by the pound. What becomes of it now is up to you, and I have waited a long time to say that to someone." A sealed letter marked "To the finder" leaned on the nearest shelf, beside a torn half of an old map. Next to them sat a small jewelled owl.

choices.label: Read the founder's sealed letter.
Fit the two halves of the torn map together.
Climb back up the stair to tell someone.
Pick up the jewelled owl as proof.

nodes.body: Nadia broke the old wax and unfolded the founder's letter. "To the finder," it began, in a thin, sloping hand. "They will have told you that I sold the town's treasures and kept the money, and I let them say it. The museum owed more than it owned, and the men it owed wanted all of this sold by the pound, so I hid it, and took the blame, and waited for the debts to die. They outlived me. My last record is waiting, friend, so key in forty, and I will show you where the whole truth is kept." Under his name ran one more line, in writing so small that it looked like a row of ants.

choices.label: Key in forty.
Keep the letter safe and leave the rest.
Read the row of ants through the founder's glasses.

nodes.body: Nadia pulled the founder's glasses down out of her hair and held the letter close, and the row of ants stood up and became words. "I have left a lamp on my reading table," it said. "If it still lights when you pull the chain, then someone has been changing the bulb for a house that never thanked them, so find that person, for they have earned a look at this room." It had to be somebody who walked this house at night, with a ring of keys and a pocket full of spare bulbs. Nadia could think of only one person.

choices.label: Key in forty.

nodes.body: She keyed in forty. "Stop forty," said the handset, "which is the last stop on this tour." There was a long crackle before Ellery spoke. "Count three shelves from the door and press where the wood is darkest," he said, "and thank you, since I did not expect to be thanked, so I am doing it first." Nadia counted and pressed, and a panel swung out to show a thick book bound in leather. Page after page, in that thin hand, he had listed every piece in the room, and beside each one he had written where it came from and where in the town it belonged.

choices.label: Read the book to the end.

nodes.body: Nadia sat on the cold floor and read the book from its first page to its last. There was a painting for the town hall and a clock for the school. There was a carved saint for the chapel on the hill, with a note beside her: "They will say I stole her, so put her back and say nothing." Line by line, the thief the town remembered faded away. In his place stood a man with a ledger and a secret and nobody to tell. By the time gray light came down the stair, she knew where every piece in the room should go.

choices.label: Carry the whole truth up into the morning.

nodes.body: Nadia folded the letter along its old creases and slid it into her coat, and she left every shelf as she had found it. A man had kept this secret for a lifetime, and she was not going to spill it in one morning to the first grown-up with a clipboard. It needed the right day, and the right person, and a plan. The room had waited a hundred years, so it could wait until she had one. She climbed the stair and pushed the marble slab back into place, until the floor looked as if it had never moved.

choices.label: Slip out with the letter and a plan.

nodes.body: Nadia laid her half of the map beside the half from the shelf, and the torn edges met like two hands. Whole, the map showed what her half had only hinted at: the lost east wing, drawn room by room, bricked up but never pulled down. It was still there inside the walls, a dark piece of the museum that no tour had ever entered. A dotted line ran to it from this very room, through the back of the last shelf. Up above, the long night was wearing thin.

choices.label: Follow the dotted line to the lost wing.
Photograph the map and go.
Trace every room of the map first.
Turn the whole map over.

nodes.body: Nadia followed the dotted line to the last shelf and pushed, and it swung like a door. Behind it a brick passage ran a dozen steps and ended in old wallpaper, which tore like a page. She stepped through into a long gallery under dust sheets. Paintings hung on every wall, the ones the town had been told were sold and lost, and their colors were dim but alive under her phone's light. She did not need the handset to tell her whose rooms these were. She photographed every frame she could reach.

choices.label: Bring the lost wing to light.

nodes.body: Nadia flattened both halves and photographed the map corner to corner, twice, in case her hands had moved. Then she photographed the shelves, the sealed letter, and the number over the door. She put the shelf's half of the map back exactly where it had lain, so that nothing in the room had moved by so much as a finger. "I'll be back," she told the owl, "with people who own gloves." The owl kept its opinion to itself.

choices.label: Head out with the proof.

nodes.body: Nadia turned the whole map over and pushed the torn edges together. On her side was the brown ink she had read under the lobby lamp: "My east wing is not gone, for it has one door left, and that door opens only" and then the tear. On the other side was the rest of it: "from within, onto the garden. The key you carry fits it, so go out by my door, friend, and come back by the front one." She read it through twice. Then she looked at the small brass key, which had opened one lock tonight and had been waiting for a second. The dotted line on the front showed the way, through the back of the last shelf.

choices.label: Go out by the founder's door.

nodes.body: Nadia climbed back up the stair with the sealed letter in her hand, into the hush of the rotunda. The curator unlocked the staff door at eight. A letter addressed to the finder was the sort of proof a curator had to take seriously. Tess woke at seven, and Tess had never in her life been told a secret second. Through the open door of the guard's room lay a pad of paper and a pencil on a string. The museum had kept this room from itself for a hundred years, and it deserved the chance to find it.

choices.label: Wait at the staff door for the curator.
Tell Tess first, and nobody else.
Leave it for the museum to find.

nodes.body: Nadia waited at the staff door until the curator arrived at eight, juggling her keys and a paper cup. "We are closed," the curator said, "and how did you get in?" Nadia held out the sealed letter. "I never got out," she said. "This was in a room under the rotunda. It is addressed to the finder, which is me, but I think you should be there when it is opened." The curator looked at the wax and at the thin brown writing. Then she followed Nadia to the rotunda and looked for a long time at the open floor beside the globe. Very carefully, she put her coffee down on the marble.

choices.label: Lead the curator down the stair.

nodes.body: Nadia went to tell Tess first. She pushed the marble slab back over the stair, and when the first keys of the morning opened the staff door, she slipped out behind whoever had opened it and ran through the garden gate. Tess opened her front door in her pajamas and stared at the dust on Nadia's coat. "You went home sick," said Tess, as if Nadia might have forgotten. "I got locked in the museum," said Nadia, "and I found a room under the floor, and you are the first person I have told." Tess took that in. "Is there treasure?" she asked, and when Nadia nodded, she asked whether anybody else was allowed to know. Nadia thought of the letter in her coat, addressed to the finder. "Not yet," she said, "but I know three numbers, and I need someone to keep watch."

choices.label: Seal the secret with a promise.

nodes.body: Nadia left it for the museum to find. She went back down for the shelf's half of the map and laid both halves on the guard's desk, with the torn edges touching. On his pad she wrote, in square letters of her own: "Set the rings on the globe to four, nine, and two, and go down the stair, where everything is just as he left it." She did not sign it. The experts could do the rest, with their gloves and their cameras, the way the founder would have wanted it done. She put the sealed letter on top, where nobody could miss it, and the brass key on top of that. Then she pushed the marble slab back over the stair, so that the museum could open it for itself.

choices.label: Leave the clue and slip away.

nodes.body: The owl was no bigger than a teacup, with feathers made of amber chips and glass eyes that held what little light there was. One look at it would prove her whole wild story, with no explaining, and nobody telling her she had dreamed it. Nadia picked it up. It was heavier than it looked, and something inside it ticked once. Where it had stood, the velvet rose a hair, and a round hollow showed in it, the size of a coin, stamped with a circle crossed by two lines. Under the shelf, very softly, a spring began to wind.

choices.label: Pocket the owl and run for the stair.
Set the owl back on its velvet.
Press the brass token into the hollow.

nodes.body: Nadia pushed the owl deep into her coat pocket and ran for the stair, already picturing the look on Tess's face. She had reached the third step when the spring under the shelf let go, and a row of small bells began to ring. They were not loud, just sweet and steady and impossible to stop, like a music box for giants. Behind her the round hollow sat empty in the velvet. It had wanted something left in the owl's place, something coin-shaped, and she had nothing that shape. The ringing followed her up the stair and out across the rotunda.

choices.label: Keep running with the bells behind her.

nodes.body: Nadia set the owl back on its velvet, and the spring under the shelf stopped winding. The hollow vanished under the little amber feet, and the room was quiet again. So the shelf had been counting. She let out a breath. Her hands were empty and dusty and not in any trouble. Then she turned the coded note over, found a pencil stub in her coat, and began to write down everything in the room, shelf by shelf, starting with the owl.

choices.label: Climb back up with the list.

nodes.body: Nadia dug the brass token out of her pocket and read its four words again: "LEAVE ME WHERE YOU TAKE." She pressed it into the hollow, and it fitted like a coin in a slot. The spring under the shelf stopped winding, and something clicked shut for good. She waited, but there were no bells and no trapdoor. In her hands the owl ticked again, and when she turned it over she found a small key between its wings. She gave it three turns, and the beak opened. "I am Ambrose Ellery's owl," said the owl, in a tiny, crackling copy of the founder's voice, "so believe whoever carries me, for they came by the proper road."

choices.label: Carry the owl up to meet the curator.

nodes.body: Nadia stepped between two marble busts, lifted her chin, and held her breath like a statue. The torch beam slid along the row, over one stone face after another, and went past her, and then it came back. "That one is new," said the guard, "and it is wearing trainers." He was not unkind about it, only firm, and the badge on his jacket said PYM. On the walk to the lobby he saw the map in her hand and stopped dead. "Handset thirteen," he said softly. "I put that map in there myself, a month ago, after thirty-one years of carrying it about. Did you find what the mark opens?" Nadia shook her head, so he rang her mother from the front desk, and then he poured two mugs of tea and asked her where she would have looked.

The gallery door clicked shut behind Nadia, quiet and final, and it had no handle on the inside. The dark room held dust sheets, a ladder, and one huge arch, bricked up, with the number 29 painted on the bricks. She keyed it in. "Through this arch lies my east wing," said Ellery, "the best rooms in the house." Cold air leaked between the bricks, so the wing on her map was still back there. She sat on the ladder, lit her phone, and for the first time turned the map over. There was half a sentence in brown ink about a door, and under it a warning in square pencil letters: "Rope gallery door shuts itself, so WEDGE IT. I sat in there till the cleaners came." Nadia read it twice, and then she laughed until the dust sheets shook. The cleaners came at six.

Nadia went on in the dark and counted eleven shelves, turned, and counted nine. Somewhere after that the numbers slid away from her, and every shelf felt like the last one. She sat down on the cold floor to wait for a guard, a ghost, or morning, and morning came first. At six the lights clicked on overhead, row by row, and she saw where she was. On the shelf beside her knee sat four flat boxes of gramophone records, marked 37 to 40, with a label in a thin hand: "For the finder." Ten steps away, cut into a shelf edge, was the mark from her map. She had sat ten steps from it all night. One stub of chalk off the tour board, and one arrow on every corner, would have walked her straight to it.

Nadia gave the lid one hard pull, and the old glass let go with a crack like a starting pistol. A split ran from corner to corner, but the lid came up, and she had the ledger in her hands when the torch beam found her. The guard looked at the glass, then at her, then at the book. "Thirty-one years I have dusted that cabinet," he said, "and I never knew there was a second book in it." He turned to the ribboned page and stared at its two columns of letters. "It is the key to a code," Nadia said, and he sat down slowly on the top stair. "Then you had better tell me what it unlocks," he said, "while we wait for your mother." She told him, and he wrote down the broken glass and none of the rest, and he kept her place with the ribbon.

Nadia climbed higher into the dark dome, past the last painted star, until the bare ladder ended at a hatch. It had been bricked over so long ago that the mortar had gone black. She looked down, which was a mistake, and then she looked again, which was not. From up here the gold stars made a picture nobody could see from the floor: a circle crossed by two lines, with one star shining like brass at the end of the walkway below her. "You up there," called a voice, very calm and very far down, "stay still, because I am coming to hold the ladder." It was the night guard, and he held it the whole way. He did not shout until both her feet were on the floor.

Nadia dashed for the gap while the pendulum hung clear, and she very nearly made it. The great brass disc came back like a slow door and bumped her off her feet, firmly but not hard, and sat her down on the safe side. The key flew out of her hand. It skidded under the swing of the pendulum and rang down through a grating beyond the doorway. She lay on her back and watched the disc pass over her, in no hurry at all. There was writing on its underside, which nobody standing up would ever see. "Count to three," it said, "and walk." Somewhere under the floor, her key was still ringing.

Nadia leaned on the third ring and shoved, and it went over the mark with a crunch that she felt in her teeth. After that nothing would turn, not the third ring and not the other two. She sat down beside the silent globe with her back against the pedestal. At a quarter to four, something inside it woke up by itself. Gears she had never touched began to turn the rings toward their numbers, met the jam, and strained. The marble beside her slid back the width of a finger. Cold air came up through the crack, and by the glow of her phone she could see the top step of a stair. The clockwork tried twice more, and then it let out a long sigh, and the crack closed.

The bells led the night guard straight to her. His torch caught Nadia halfway across the rotunda, with the owl ticking away in her coat pocket like a small, guilty clock. She took it out and held it up, since there was no use pretending. "Well, now," he said, looking past her at the open floor and the stair going down, "thirty-one years I have walked over that." He took the owl in both hands, as gently as an egg. Then he sat her on the bottom step of the main stairs to wait for her mother, and he went down into the room alone. She heard him laugh, once, a long way below. A minute later the bells stopped, so he must have found where the owl belonged.

Nadia traced every room of the map with one finger, and then every corridor, and then the lost wing twice. It had nine windows down its garden side, each one drawn with a tiny cross. When she looked up at last, gray light was coming down the stair, and she could hear the first keys of the morning in the staff door. She put the shelf's half of the map back and slipped out through the garden gate before anyone saw her. On the pavement she stopped and counted the museum's windows along that side. There were nine, and the last of them was dusty and dark. She had passed the lost wing on the way to school every week of her life.

Nadia wound the brass wren, and it shook itself, hopped twice along the bench, and sang three notes as thin as wire. Then it bowed, as if somebody had taught it manners, and she laughed out loud in the dusty room. She photographed every bench and every half-built creature, and she touched nothing else. When morning light came through the rotunda dome, she was waiting on the bench by the staff door with the wren in her cupped hands. The curator was not going to believe a word about a workshop hidden behind the globe. But the wren could sing, and it could bow, and the low door was still open.

Her mum said she would be there in forty minutes. It took Nadia ten to walk the old guard to the rotunda and show him the pin on the floor. He read the numbers off the note, because his eyes were better at paper than his knees were at kneeling, and she set the rings to four, nine, and two. The marble slid back. He stood at the top of the stair he had hunted for thirty-one years, and he did not go down it. "After you," he said, "since I only kept the map warm." They went down together, by the glow of her phone and the beam of his torch. When her mum came through the front doors, the two of them were sitting on the top step, arguing about who got to tell the curator.

With the letter in one hand and the book under her arm, Nadia climbed the last stair into a morning brighter than any she remembered. The night guard was the first person she met, coming across the rotunda with his torch still on. She did not say a word. She held the book open at the first page and watched him read the founder's writing, and she watched his face. By noon the curator had read it too. By the end of the month the saint was back in the chapel on the hill, the clock was ticking in the school hall, and a new brass plate hung under the portrait of old Ellery. It had only three words on it: "NOT A THIEF."

Nadia slipped out of the staff door with the first keys of the morning, the founder's letter folded in her coat. Over the next weeks she went to work on the curator, one small question at a time. Had the museum ever checked what was under the rotunda? Was it true that old Ellery sold the town's treasures, or had anyone ever seen a receipt? She left a copy of one page of the letter in the suggestions box, with no name on it. By the end of the month the curator was reading old account books over lunch. On the first day of the holidays, Nadia found her kneeling by the globe with a torch, counting the numbers on the rings. "Four, nine, two," said Nadia, and waited to be asked how she knew.

By Friday the lost wing belonged to everybody. Nadia's photographs brought the curator first. Then came two experts in white gloves, and a reporter who spelled her name wrong. Then the bricks came out of an old arch in a roped-off gallery, and the town walked through into rooms that had been shut for a hundred years. People stood in front of paintings their grandparents had described, and cried a little, and said they had dust in their eyes. Nadia stood at the back with an audio guide around her neck. The museum had put up a new plaque in the first room, and she keyed in its number, although she already knew whose voice would answer.

The lost wing was a long gallery under dust sheets, hung with paintings the town thought it had lost. Nadia walked its whole length with her phone held high and did not touch a thing. At the far end stood a narrow door with a keyhole cut like the mark on her map, and the key turned as if it had been oiled yesterday. Cold morning air came in, with birdsong and the smell of wet grass. She stepped out into the museum garden, locked the founder's door behind her, and walked round to the front. At nine o'clock she was first in line. "One, please," she told the woman at the ticket desk, "and I need to see the curator, because I have something of hers."

The curator came through the staff door at eight with her keys in her teeth and her coat half off. She found a dusty girl sitting on the bench, holding a jewelled owl. "That had better be from the gift shop," the curator said. Nadia shook her head and said, "It's from a room under the rotunda." The curator sighed and told her, "There is no room under the rotunda." Nadia wound the key three turns. "I am Ambrose Ellery's owl," said the owl, "so believe whoever carries me." The curator sat down on the bench rather suddenly and looked at the owl for a long time. "Cancel my nine o'clock," she said, to nobody at all, and held out a hand for Nadia to lead the way.

The curator went down the stair first and came back up a different person. By midmorning there were white gloves, two cameras, and a man from the town hall who kept saying "good heavens" to nobody. They opened the letter together at the reading table upstairs, and the curator read it out in a voice that wobbled a little at the end. Old Ellery had not sold the town's treasures, and here they all were. Somebody fetched Nadia a chair, a sandwich, and a telephone to ring her mother. She sat in the middle of the fuss, dusty and yawning. The audio guide still hung around her neck. "Stop one," she told it quietly, and keyed it in to hear him say it again.

They went back on the next school visit, two girls who seemed very interested in the big brass globe. Tess kept watch for the guard while Nadia set the rings, and for one minute the two of them stood on the top step of the hidden stair and looked down into the dark. Then they closed it up again. It was Tess who said they should hand the letter over on the last day of term, and Tess who made them both spit on it. Until then the room under the rotunda had two keepers, a password, and a rota. Nadia had the odd feeling that old Ellery would have liked the rota best.

Nadia slipped out of the staff door the moment the first keys of the morning had opened it, and she was through the garden gate before anyone saw her. Nothing happened for four days. On the fifth, the museum shut without warning, vans came, and the newspaper ran a photograph of the curator on the hidden stair with her mouth open. Nobody asked Nadia a thing. When her class went back the next month, the room under the rotunda had a rope, a guide, and a queue. There was a new brass plaque by the globe, and she read it twice: "Found by a curious visitor, who did not leave a name." The night guard was on the door that day. As her class filed past, he looked down at her trainers, and then he winked.

Nadia dialed the rest of the number, and her mum answered on the second ring. "It's me, and I'm fine," Nadia said, "but I'm not at Tess's." There was a silence, then a great many questions, and then the sound of car keys. Nadia sat in the guard's chair to wait and wrote three numbers on the back of her hand. The guard found her there when he came in for a fresh crossword. He looked at the girl in his chair, at the pin on the rotunda floor, and at the brass key on his desk. "I think," he said, sitting down on the edge of the desk, "that you had better start at the beginning." So she did, and he was still asking questions when the headlights swung across the front doors.

When the first keys of the morning opened the staff door, Nadia slipped out behind whoever had opened it and through the garden gate into the gray dawn, with the whole map safe on her phone. At nine she came back through the front doors like any other visitor and asked to see the curator. The curator looked at the first photograph for a long time, and at the second for longer. "Where did you take these?" she asked at last. Nadia told her about the globe, the three numbers, and the stair. "I left everything where it was," she said, "because I thought you would want to see it the way he left it." The curator was already reaching for her keys.

Nadia climbed back up with her list, forty lines of it, in pencil on the back of a coded note. She had not opened the letter or touched the map, and the owl sat where it had always sat. At eight the curator came through the staff door, and Nadia stood up from the bench and held the list out. The curator read the first line, and then the second, and then she sat down. "A jewelled owl," she said slowly, "on a shelf that counts. Nobody could make that up." Nadia thought it over before she answered. "I could have made up the owl," she said, "but never a shelf that counts." The curator folded the list into her pocket and went to fetch a torch.
